claim: Recent studies using fast-freeze electron microscopy and capacitance measurements reported an ultrafast mode of endocytosis operating at physiological temperatures.
source: Recent studies using fast-freeze electron microscopy and capacitance measurements reported an ultrafast mode of endocytosis operating at physiological temperatures.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work using specific methodologies (fast-freeze EM and capacitance measurements).

claim: Three components of retrieval operate at ultrafast (~150–250 ms, ~20% of events), fast (~5–12 s, ~40% of events) and ultraslow speeds (>20 s, ~40% of events).
source: In this setting, we could distinguish three components of retrieval operating at ultrafast (~150–250 ms, ~20% of events), fast (~5–12 s, ~40% of events) and ultraslow speeds (>20 s, ~40% of events).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from optical monitoring of single synaptic vesicle endocytosis.

claim: Increasing Ca2+ slowed the fast events.
source: While increasing Ca2+ slowed the fast events, increasing temperature accelerated their time course.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements comparing different Ca2+ concentrations.

claim: Increasing temperature accelerated the time course of fast events.
source: While increasing Ca2+ slowed the fast events, increasing temperature accelerated their time course.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements comparing different temperatures.

claim: The kinetics of ultrafast events were only mildly affected by Ca2+ and temperature manipulations.
source: In contrast, the kinetics of ultrafast events were only mildly affected by these manipulations.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing ultrafast event kinetics under different conditions.

claim: Early studies using electron microscopy and FM dyes postulated retrieval and recycling of synaptic vesicles to occur within 30—90 s.
source: Early studies using electron microscopy (EM) and fluorescence imaging with FM dyes postulated retrieval and recycling of synaptic vesicles to occur within 30—90 s (Miller and Heuser, 1984; Ryan et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies using EM and FM dyes.

claim: Subsequent experiments proposed a faster time course — spanning only about 2 s — for synaptic vesicle endocytosis based on capacitance measurements.
source: However, subsequent experiments proposed a faster time course — spanning only about 2 s — for synaptic vesicle endocytosis based on capacitance measurements (von Gersdorff and Matthews, 1994), a time course also corroborated by FM dye-based studies (Klingauf et al., 1998; Kavalali et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to capacitance measurement studies.

claim: Experiments using fast-freeze EM or improved capacitance measurements produced estimates within 100—500 ms for synaptic vesicle retrieval in central synapses.
source: In recent years, experiments using fast-freeze EM (Watanabe et al., 2013) or improved capacitance measurements (Delvendahl et al., 2016) produced estimates within 100—500 ms for synaptic vesicle retrieval in central synapses.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to recent fast-freeze EM and capacitance measurement studies.

claim: Ultrafast synaptic endocytosis appeared to predominantly occur near physiological temperatures (~36°C).
source: This so-called ultrafast synaptic endocytosis appeared to predominantly occur near physiological temperatures (~36°C) (Watanabe and Boucrot, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work on temperature dependence of ultrafast endocytosis.

claim: Experiments using synaptic vesicle proteins labeled with pHluorin to optically monitor single synaptic vesicle endocytosis gave rise to variable and often contradicting results.
source: In contrast, experiments using synaptic vesicle proteins labeled with pHluorin (a pH-sensitive derivative of GFP) to optically monitor single synaptic vesicle endocytosis gave rise to variable and often contradicting results (Balaji and Ryan, 2007; Gandhi and Stevens, 2003; Granseth et al., 2006; Leitz and Kavalali, 2011; Zhu et al., 2009) with the extra complication that these studies were typically conducted at room temperature.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple pHluorin-based studies showing variable results.

claim: The vesicular glutamate transporter 1 (vGluT1) bound to pHluorin has been widely used to track synaptic vesicle trafficking based on its low plasma membrane expression and high signal-to-noise ratio.
source: The vesicular glutamate transporter 1 (vGluT1) bound to the pH sensitive derivative of GFP, pHluorin has been widely used to track synaptic vesicle trafficking based on its low plasma membrane expression and high signal-to-noise ratio (Voglmaier et al., 2006; Balaji and Ryan, 2007; Leitz and Kavalali, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies using vGluT1-pHluorin.

claim: At room temperature (~24°C), increasing extracellular Ca2+ concentration from 2 mM to 8 mM leads to an increase in the number of fused vesicles and a slight increase in the decay time.
source: At room temperature (~24°C), increasing extracellular Ca2+ concentration from 2 mM to 8 mM leads to an increase in the number of fused vesicles (seen as an increase in peak amplitude) and a slight increase in the decay time, suggesting saturation of the endocytic machinery under strong, repetitive stimulation (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A-C.

claim: At physiological temperatures (34–36°C) the time course of bulk synaptic vesicle endocytosis seen after strong stimulation shows accelerated kinetics.
source: Earlier studies have demonstrated that at physiological temperatures (34–36°C) the time course of bulk synaptic vesicle endocytosis seen after strong stimulation shows accelerated kinetics (Fernández-Alfonso and Ryan, 2004; Renden and von Gersdorff, 2007; Soykan et al., 2017) possibly via activation of ultrafast endocytosis mechanisms (Delvendahl et al., 2016; Watanabe et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies on temperature-dependent endocytosis kinetics.

claim: Increasing the temperature from ~24 to 34°C led to a ~ 2.5 fold decrease in the fluorescence decay time constants after 40 Hz stimulation.
source: In agreement with this premise, in our experiments, increasing the temperature from ~24 to 34°C led to a ~ 2.5 fold decrease in the fluorescence decay time constants after 40 Hz stimulation (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: At 34°C faster fluorescence rise times at stimulation onset were observed compared to room temperature.
source: Moreover, at 34°C we observed faster fluorescence rise times at stimulation onset compared to room temperature (Figure 1D), consistent with an increase in the synchronicity of release seen in previous electrophysiological studies (Pyott and Rosenmund, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and citation to prior electrophysiology work.

claim: For action potential evoked release the kinetics of endocytosis is negatively regulated by Ca2+ concentration in a synaptotagmin-dependent manner.
source: For action potential (AP) evoked release the kinetics of this process is negatively regulated by Ca2+ concentration in a synaptotagmin-dependent manner (Leitz and Kavalali, 2011; Li et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies on Ca2+ and synaptotagmin regulation.

claim: A time-domain de-noising algorithm based on methods originally developed to de-noise electrophysiological single channel recordings was used.
source: Moreover, we increased the time resolution of our measurements, by a combination of faster image acquisition settings and time-domain de-noising of fluorescence signals based on methods originally developed to de-noise electrophysiological single channel recordings (Chung and Kennedy, 1991).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to the original de-noising method.

claim: The non-linear de-noising algorithm preserves the amplitude of the measured signal without major distortion of the edges compared to other classical methods based on the fast Fourier transform.
source: This type of noise reduction preserves the amplitude of the measured signal without major distortion of the edges compared to other classical methods based on the fast Fourier transform (see Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The experimental noise shows a Gaussian distribution.
source: As the filtering method we used assumes Gaussian distribution of the noise (Chung and Kennedy, 1991), we first validated that our experimental noise shows a Gaussian distribution (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by validation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: In negative imaging controls with no stimulation in the presence of TTX or in 0 mM extracellular Ca2+ following EGTA-AM treatment, events were detected with a probability of ~0.03% or less.
source: In these control experiments, we detected events with a probability of ~0.03% or less (likely reflecting false positives along with spontaneous fusion events), well within acceptable boundaries (~5 fold less than typical event detection rate under normal conditions) (Figure 2D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by negative control data shown in Figure 2D–E.

claim: Mean release probability at 2 mM extracellular Ca2+ is ~0.15.
source: As shown in Figure 3B and C, mean release probability at 2 mM extracellular Ca2+ is ~0.15, in agreement with previous reports (Leitz and Kavalali, 2011; Murthy et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and C and citations to prior reports.

claim: Increasing Ca2+ concentration to 8 mM leads to a marked increase in release probability.
source: Increasing Ca2+ concentration to 8 mM leads to a marked increase in release probability (Figure 3B–C), although switching from room temperature (~24°C) to 34°C, did not result in a major change in release probability, consistent with previous electrophysiological measurements (Kushmerick et al., 2006; Pyott and Rosenmund, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B–C and citations to prior electrophysiology studies.

claim: Switching from room temperature (~24°C) to 34°C did not result in a major change in release probability.
source: Increasing Ca2+ concentration to 8 mM leads to a marked increase in release probability (Figure 3B–C), although switching from room temperature (~24°C) to 34°C, did not result in a major change in release probability, consistent with previous electrophysiological measurements (Kushmerick et al., 2006; Pyott and Rosenmund, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B–C and citations to prior electrophysiology studies.

claim: 40 ± 2% of all fusion events did not return to baseline during the course of imaging (>20 s).
source: Initially, we detected that 40 ± 2% of all fusion events did not return to baseline during the course of imaging (>20 s, and see Figure 3H) suggesting an ultraslow pathway for endocytosis (Gandhi and Stevens, 2003; Zhu et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H and citations to prior studies.

claim: The dwell time distributions are best represented by a double exponential decay function.
source: Further analysis of the histograms revealed that they are best represented by a double exponential decay function, pointing to the co-existence of two endocytic mechanisms with different mean rates.
evidence: The claim is supported by mathematical fitting of experimental data distributions.

claim: The fitting of dwell time distributions revealed an ultrafast endocytic component with an average time course of about 150–250 ms.
source: The fitting of dwell time distributions for the experimental groups revealed an ultrafast endocytic component with an average time course of about 150–250 ms, and a fast process that proceeds with an order of magnitude slower time course of around 5–12 s (arrows in Figure 3D–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by exponential fitting of experimental data shown in Figure 3D–G.

claim: A fast endocytic process proceeds with a time course of around 5–12 s.
source: The fitting of dwell time distributions for the experimental groups revealed an ultrafast endocytic component with an average time course of about 150–250 ms, and a fast process that proceeds with an order of magnitude slower time course of around 5–12 s (arrows in Figure 3D–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by exponential fitting of experimental data shown in Figure 3D–G.

claim: Increasing extracellular Ca2+ concentration from 2 to 8 mM led to only a 10–15% slowdown of ultrafast endocytosis at both temperatures.
source: Increasing extracellular Ca2+ concentration from 2 to 8 mM led to only a 10–15% slowdown of ultrafast endocytosis at both temperatures (Figure 3D–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D–G.

claim: Increasing extracellular calcium concentration from 2 to 8 mM led to a ~ 60% slowdown of fast endocytosis at 24°C.
source: The fast component of endocytosis, on the other hand, showed a steeper temperature dependence. Increasing extracellular calcium concentration from 2 to 8 mM led to a ~ 60% slowdown of fast endocytosis at 24°C, while increasing calcium at 34°C led to only a ~ 10% slowdown (Figure 3D–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D–G.

claim: Increasing calcium at 34°C led to only a ~ 10% slowdown of fast endocytosis.
source: The fast component of endocytosis, on the other hand, showed a steeper temperature dependence. Increasing extracellular calcium concentration from 2 to 8 mM led to a ~ 60% slowdown of fast endocytosis at 24°C, while increasing calcium at 34°C led to only a ~ 10% slowdown (Figure 3D–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D–G.

claim: The relative contribution of each mode to total protein retrieval did not change significantly under different conditions.
source: While the mean speed of endocytosis for both fast and ultrafast pathways was regulated by temperature and Ca2+, the relative contribution of each mode to total protein retrieval did not change significantly (Figure 3H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Under all conditions around 40% of fusion events were not followed by endocytosis in the imaging period (>20 s).
source: Overall under all conditions around 40% of fusion events were not followed by endocytosis in the imaging period (>20 s), 13–18% undergo ultrafast endocytosis and 38–48% of vGluT1-pHluorins were retrieved through a slow pathway (Figure 3H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: 13–18% of events undergo ultrafast endocytosis.
source: Overall under all conditions around 40% of fusion events were not followed by endocytosis in the imaging period (>20 s), 13–18% undergo ultrafast endocytosis and 38–48% of vGluT1-pHluorins were retrieved through a slow pathway (Figure 3H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: 38–48% of vGluT1-pHluorins were retrieved through a slow pathway.
source: Overall under all conditions around 40% of fusion events were not followed by endocytosis in the imaging period (>20 s), 13–18% undergo ultrafast endocytosis and 38–48% of vGluT1-pHluorins were retrieved through a slow pathway (Figure 3H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Averaged non-denoised traces showed two phases of fluorescence decay with ultrafast (~250 ms) and fast kinetics (~3–7 s).
source: In addition, to test whether the two components of retrieval we identified were a consequence of denoising, we averaged non-denoised traces in an unbiased manner and found two phases of fluorescence decay with ultrafast (~250 ms) and fast kinetics (~3–7 s) (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of averaged non-denoised traces shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In neurons where synaptotagmin-1 (syt1) was knocked-down the fast component is greatly reduced and vGluT1-pHluorin is retrieved almost exclusively by ultrafast endocytosis (70–80% of all fusion events).
source: Interestingly, in neurons where the Ca2+ sensor synaptotagmin-1 (syt1) was knocked-down (KD) the fast component is greatly reduced and vGluT1-pHluorin is retrieved almost exclusively by ultrafast endocytosis (70–80% of all fusion events, Figure 4B–C), suggesting that ultrafast endocytosis is syt1-independent (see Li et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from syt1 KD neurons shown in Figure 4B–C and citation to prior work.

claim: Ultraslow retrieval (>20 s) is abolished in syt1 KD neurons.
source: Moreover, ultraslow retrieval (>20 s) is also abolished in syt1 KD neurons (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from syt1 KD neurons shown in Figure 4C.

claim: For synaptotagmin-7 (syt7) KD neurons, averaged single vesicle traces showed a double exponential decay (τ1 = 0.31 ± 0.05 s, τ2 = 8.5 ± 4.8 s) similarly to control synapses.
source: This was not the case for synaptotagmin-7 (syt7) KD neurons, where averaged single vesicle traces showed a double exponential decay (τ1 = 0.31 ± 0.05 s, τ2 = 8.5 ± 4.8 s) similarly to control synapses.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from syt7 KD neurons.

claim: Approximately 60% of total fusion events displayed dwell times and subsequent decay.
source: Approximately 60% of total fusion events displayed dwell times and subsequent decay.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations of fusion events.

claim: In 50% of events that displayed dwell times, the fluorescence returned back to baseline completely, consistent with full quantal retrieval of vGluT1-pHluorins (fractional retrieval of 1.0 ± 0.2).
source: Among these, only in 50% the fluorescence returned back to baseline completely, consistent with full quantal retrieval of vGluT1-pHluorins (fractional retrieval of 1.0 ± 0.2, see Figure 4D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D–E.

claim: Approximately 35% of the fusion events that were followed by a measurable dwell time showed partial retrieval.
source: Approximately, 35% of the fusion events that were followed by a measurable dwell time, showed partial retrieval, indicating that some vGluT1-pHluorin molecules might diffuse away from the site of fusion and are temporarily unavailable for endocytosis.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations of partial retrieval events.

claim: The remaining ~15% of events showed excess retrieval, suggesting that more vGluT1-pHluorin molecules were retrieved compared to the ones that fused.
source: The remaining ~15% of events showed excess retrieval, suggesting that more vGluT1-pHluorin molecules were retrieved compared to the ones that fused (Figure 4D–E), similar to what was described in other systems (e.g. Chung and Kavalali, 2009; Van Hook and Thoreson, 2012; Zhu et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D–E and citations to similar findings in other systems.

claim: The dispersion of retrieval values increased with longer dwell times.
source: Plotting the fraction of retrieval for each fusion event as a function of the duration of its dwell time revealed that the dispersion of retrieval values increased with longer dwell times (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: For syt1 KD neurons, ~80% of vGluT1-pHluorin fusion events showed quantal retrieval (1.0 ± 0.2).
source: As mentioned before, for neurons lacking syt1 the majority of fusion events were followed by ultrafast endocytosis, for these events vGluT1-pHluorin is endocytosed very efficiently, with ~80% of vGluT1-pHluorin fusion events showing quantal retrieval (1.0 ± 0.2, Figure 4G–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from syt1 KD neurons shown in Figure 4G–H.

claim: Ultrafast endocytosis is Ca2+, syt1 and temperature independent.
source: Our results suggest that ultrafast endocytosis is Ca2+, syt1 and temperature independent, and it rapidly retrieves approximately the same amount of protein that fused.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing minimal effects of Ca2+, syt1 KD, and temperature on ultrafast endocytosis kinetics.

claim: Distinct synaptic vesicle proteins are typically coupled to diverse endocytic mechanisms.
source: Distinct synaptic vesicle proteins are typically coupled to diverse endocytic mechanisms (Chanaday and Kavalali, 2017; Li et al., 2017; Pan et al., 2015; Voglmaier and Edwards, 2007)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies on protein-specific endocytic mechanisms.

claim: At 40 Hz stimulation, the increase of temperature from 24 to 34°C caused a ~ 2.5 fold rise in the bulk endocytic rate of Syp1-pHTomato.
source: At 40 Hz stimulation, the increase of temperature from 24 to 34°C caused a ~ 2.5 fold rise in the bulk endocytic rate of Syp1-pHTomato (Figure 5B) coupled with a faster signal rise time (Figure 5C), consistent with our observations using vGluT1-pHluorin.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and 5C.

claim: At the single vesicle level, release probability did not change in response to increase in temperature (~0.15 at both tested temperatures) for Syp1-pHTomato.
source: At the single vesicle level, as before, we did not detect a change in release probability in response to increase in temperature (~0.15 at both tested temperatures) (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Histograms of detectable dwell times for Syp1-pHTomato (50 ± 2% of events) were best fitted with a double exponential, revealing the presence of two parallel endocytic processes.
source: Histograms of detectable dwell times (50 ± 2% of events) were best fitted with a double exponential, revealing the presence of two parallel endocytic processes for synaptophysin (Figure 5F–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by exponential fitting of experimental data shown in Figure 5F–I.

claim: The mean time courses of the two endocytic processes for synaptophysin were about 175–300 ms and 5–11 s.
source: The mean time courses of these two processes were about 175–300 ms and 5–11 s, comparable to our previous results with vGluT1-pHluorin (arrows in Figure 5F–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by exponential fitting of experimental data shown in Figure 5F–I.

claim: The increase in temperature did not produce a significant effect in the overall endocytic rate at 2 mM Ca2+ for Syp1-pHTomato.
source: While the increase in temperature did not produce a significant effect in the overall endocytic rate at 2 mM Ca2+ (Figure 5F–G, and inset in 5G), it caused an almost two-fold acceleration of retrieval at 8 mM extracellular Ca2+ (Figure 5H–I, and inset in 5I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F–G.

claim: Temperature increase caused an almost two-fold acceleration of Syp1-pHTomato retrieval at 8 mM extracellular Ca2+.
source: While the increase in temperature did not produce a significant effect in the overall endocytic rate at 2 mM Ca2+ (Figure 5F–G, and inset in 5G), it caused an almost two-fold acceleration of retrieval at 8 mM extracellular Ca2+ (Figure 5H–I, and inset in 5I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H–I.

claim: VGluT1 proteins are present in high copy numbers on synaptic vesicles (~9 per vesicle).
source: VGluT1 and Syp1 proteins are present in high copy numbers on synaptic vesicles (~9 and~31 per vesicle, respectively) (Takamori et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior quantitative study of synaptic vesicle protein copy numbers.

claim: Syp1 proteins are present in high copy numbers on synaptic vesicles (~31 per vesicle).
source: VGluT1 and Syp1 proteins are present in high copy numbers on synaptic vesicles (~9 and~31 per vesicle, respectively) (Takamori et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior quantitative study of synaptic vesicle protein copy numbers.

claim: About 40% of all vGluT1-pHluorin events do not show protein retrieval during the recording period.
source: In our experiments, about 40% of all vGluT1-pHluorin events and 50% of Syp1-pHTomato events do not show protein retrieval during the recording period, probably reflecting fully collapsed vesicles after fusion (ultraslow retrieval events).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations of non-retrieved events.

claim: About 50% of Syp1-pHTomato events do not show protein retrieval during the recording period.
source: In our experiments, about 40% of all vGluT1-pHluorin events and 50% of Syp1-pHTomato events do not show protein retrieval during the recording period, probably reflecting fully collapsed vesicles after fusion (ultraslow retrieval events).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations of non-retrieved events.

claim: V-ATPase and its subunits show low levels of expression in synapses and they have a low copy number per synaptic vesicle (~1).
source: V-ATPase and its subunits show low levels of expression in synapses and they have a low copy number per synaptic vesicle (~1) (Takamori et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior quantitative study of synaptic vesicle protein copy numbers.

claim: About 10–30% of V0a1-pHluorin co-localizes with the presynaptic marker Synapsin-1.
source: Co-localization experiments revealed that V0a1-pHluorin is properly trafficked to synapses, with about 10–30% of the probe co-localizing with the presynaptic marker Synapsin-1, also showing a similar subcellular distribution to the endogenous V0a1 protein (Figure 6A–B) and similar to what was described previously (Bagh et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-localization data shown in Figure 6A–B and citation to prior work.

claim: V0a1 over-expression or V0a1-pHluorin expression did not produce significant alterations in synaptic transmission.
source: V0a1 over-expression or V0a1-pHluorin expression did not produce significant alterations in synaptic transmission, as indicated by similar to control single AP evoked response amplitudes and charge transfer, as well as similar paired-pulse ratios (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: V0a1-pHluorin expression had no effect on spontaneous, miniature excitatory postsynaptic current (mEPSC) amplitudes and frequency.
source: V0a1-pHluorin expression also had no effect on spontaneous, miniature excitatory postsynaptic current (mEPSC) amplitudes and frequency, and only caused a 2-fold increase in miniature inhibitory postsynaptic currents (mIPSC) frequency, with no changes in amplitude (Figure 6C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6C–E.

claim: V0a1-pHluorin expression caused a 2-fold increase in miniature inhibitory postsynaptic currents (mIPSC) frequency, with no changes in amplitude.
source: V0a1-pHluorin expression also had no effect on spontaneous, miniature excitatory postsynaptic current (mEPSC) amplitudes and frequency, and only caused a 2-fold increase in miniature inhibitory postsynaptic currents (mIPSC) frequency, with no changes in amplitude (Figure 6C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6C–E.

claim: The subcellular distribution of V0a1-pHluorin was highly variable among synapses, with ~40% of the probe present in internal organelles and ~60% on the plasma membrane on average.
source: The subcellular distribution was highly variable among synapses, with ~40% of the probe present in internal organelles and ~60% on the plasma membrane on average, resembling what was described for endogenous V0a1 (Morel et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of V0a1-pHluorin distribution and citation to prior work on endogenous V0a1.

claim: The distribution of V0a1-pHluorin dwell times at 34°C could be fitted with a double exponential decay, reflecting ultrafast and fast time constants of ~250–300 ms and 3–10 s, respectively.
source: The distribution of V0a1-pHluorin dwell times at 34°C could be fitted with a double exponential decay, again reflecting ultrafast and fast time constants of ~250–300 ms and 3–10 s, respectively (Figure 6J–K).
evidence: The claim is supported by exponential fitting of experimental data shown in Figure 6J–K.

claim: For V0a1-pHluorin, the time scale of the fast component of endocytosis was more sensitive to changes in extracellular Ca2+ concentration, showing more than two-fold decrease in speed compared to a ~ 30% slow down of the ultrafast component.
source: As observed with the previous indicators, the time scale of the fast component of endocytosis was more sensitive to changes in extracellular Ca2+ concentration, showing more than two-fold decrease in speed compared to a ~ 30% slow down of the ultrafast component.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing different Ca2+ concentrations for V0a1-pHluorin.

claim: The distribution of dwell times calculated at 40 Hz imaging speed closely resembled those obtained at 10 Hz, with a peak at 200 ms and a double exponential behavior.
source: The distribution of dwell times calculated at 40 Hz imaging speed closely resembled those obtained at 10 Hz, with a peak at 200 ms and a double exponential behavior (Figure 7B–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of experimental data at different imaging speeds shown in Figure 7B–E.

claim: The mean endocytic speed for the ultrafast component at 40 Hz imaging is ~150–250 ms, 3–5 times higher than the Nyquist limit.
source: The mean endocytic speed for the ultrafast component of the distribution is ~150–250 ms, 3–5 times higher than the Nyquist limit.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements at 40 Hz imaging speed and comparison to Nyquist limit.

claim: At 24°C there is a ~50 and ~60% increase in decay time at 8 mM Ca2+ for the ultrafast and fast components, respectively.
source: As observed before, at both 24°C and 34°C, endocytosis is slowed down by higher Ca2+ concentration, although this effect is more pronounced at room temperature and particularly for the fast endocytic component (at 24°C there is a ~50 and ~60% increase in decay time at 8 mM Ca2+ for the ultrafast and fast components, respectively, while at 34°C the change is ~20 and ~40%, respectively; see arrows in Figure 7B–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B–E.

claim: At 34°C the change in decay time at 8 mM Ca2+ is ~20 and ~40% for the ultrafast and fast components, respectively.
source: As observed before, at both 24°C and 34°C, endocytosis is slowed down by higher Ca2+ concentration, although this effect is more pronounced at room temperature and particularly for the fast endocytic component (at 24°C there is a ~50 and ~60% increase in decay time at 8 mM Ca2+ for the ultrafast and fast components, respectively, while at 34°C the change is ~20 and ~40%, respectively; see arrows in Figure 7B–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B–E.

claim: The ultrafast endocytosis mechanism occurs at an average speed of ~150–300 ms, consistent with the recent flash-and-freeze electron microscopy-based estimates of ultrafast endocytosis in hippocampal synapses.
source: Our measurements suggest that the ultrafast endocytic mechanism occurs at an average speed of ~150–300 ms, consistent with the recent flash-and-freeze electron microscopy-based estimates of ultrafast endocytosis in hippocampal synapses (Watanabe et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements and citation to prior EM-based estimates.

claim: The fastest speed at which synaptic vesicle proteins can be fully retrieved after exocytosis seems to be ~150 ms.
source: Importantly, the fastest speed at which synaptic vesicle proteins can be fully retrieved after exocytosis seems to be ~150 ms, since the probability distribution of dwell times shows a dramatic reduction for shorter times.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the probability distribution of dwell times showing a dramatic reduction below 150 ms.

claim: The mean speed of ultrafast endocytosis was only mildly affected either by changes in temperature or Ca2+ concentration.
source: In our measurements, the mean speed of ultrafast endocytosis was only mildly affected either by changes in temperature or Ca2+ concentration, suggesting that the underlying molecular mechanism is insensitive to these factors and probably already operating at the limiting speed.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing minimal effects of temperature and Ca2+ on ultrafast endocytosis kinetics.

claim: The vast majority of ultrafast endocytotic events showed quantal retrieval — that is the same number of proteins that fused were retrieved.
source: The vast majority of ultrafast endocytotic events in our experiments showed quantal retrieval — that is the same number of proteins that fused were retrieved — indicating that synaptic vesicle molecular identity can be conserved through ultrafast endocytosis.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations of retrieval fractions for ultrafast events.

claim: One possible mechanism underlying quantal retrieval could be the re-closure of the fusion pore (compatible with kiss-and-run) where proteins remain on the synaptic vesicle membrane and are unable to diffuse away to the plasma membrane.
source: One possible mechanism underlying this observation could be the re-closure of the fusion pore (compatible with kiss-and-run) where proteins remain on the synaptic vesicle membrane and are unable to diffuse away to the plasma membrane (Alabi and Tsien, 2013).
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation of the quantal retrieval observation, supported by citation to prior work on kiss-and-run.

claim: The high efficiency in protein retrieval during ultrafast endocytosis could also be explained by a mechanism where synaptic vesicle components, lipids and proteins, remain clustered in the plasma membrane after fusion.
source: Additionally, the high efficiency in protein retrieval during ultrafast endocytosis could also be explained by a mechanism where synaptic vesicle components, lipids and proteins, remain clustered in the plasma membrane after fusion as was proposed previously (Bennett et al., 1992; Willig et al., 2006; Opazo and Rizzoli, 2010).
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to prior work on protein clustering.

claim: At the level of single vesicle retrieval, Ca2+ appears to predominantly target fast events that occur in the order of seconds but leave the time course of ultrafast events relatively unperturbed.
source: Our results showed that at the level of single vesicle retrieval, Ca2+ appears to predominantly target fast events that occur in the order of seconds but leave the time course of ultrafast events relatively unperturbed.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing differential effects of Ca2+ on fast versus ultrafast events.

claim: Synaptotagmins, besides their role in coupling fusion to Ca2+ signals, can also regulate the endocytic time course of single vesicle fusion events in a Ca2+-dependent manner.
source: Recent work from our group showed that synaptotagmins, besides their role in coupling fusion to Ca2+ signals, can also regulate the endocytic time course of single vesicle fusion events in a Ca2+-dependent manner (Leitz and Kavalali, 2016; Li et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to recent work from the authors' group.

claim: In the absence of syt1, ~80% of endocytosis occurs only through a rapid retrieval mechanism – less than 1 s – with no detectable delays.
source: Particularly, in the absence of the main Ca2+-sensor for synchronous release, syt1, ~80% of endocytosis occurs only through a rapid retrieval mechanism – less than 1 s – with no detectable delays (also see Li et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from syt1 KD neurons and citation to prior work.

claim: In the absence of syt1 very limited excess or partial retrieval of synaptic vesicle proteins was detected.
source: Moreover, in the absence of syt1 we detected very limited excess or partial retrieval of synaptic vesicle proteins.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations in syt1 KD neurons.

claim: The syt1-dependent delay in vesicle retrieval kinetics also to some extent disrupts the fidelity of vesicle protein retrieval, possibly facilitating the generation of vesicles with diverse protein compositions during retrieval.
source: This finding suggests that the syt1-dependent delay in vesicle retrieval kinetics also to some extent disrupts the fidelity of vesicle protein retrieval, possibly facilitating the generation of vesicles with diverse protein compositions during retrieval (Crawford and Kavalali, 2015; Raingo et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the syt1 KD results, supported by citations to prior work on vesicle protein composition diversity.

claim: The kinetics of single vesicle protein retrieval are not altered by syt7 knock down.
source: Furthermore, the kinetics of single vesicle protein retrieval are not altered by syt7 knock down and knocking down syt7 on top of syt1 KD does not further accelerates endocytosis (Li et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work on syt7 KD effects.

claim: Knocking down syt7 on top of syt1 KD does not further accelerate endocytosis.
source: Furthermore, the kinetics of single vesicle protein retrieval are not altered by syt7 knock down and knocking down syt7 on top of syt1 KD does not further accelerates endocytosis (Li et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work on double KD effects.

claim: Ultrafast endocytosis is relatively syt1 and Ca2+-independent, while fast endocytosis might be regulated by these factors.
source: Taken together, these results raise the possibility that ultrafast endocytosis is relatively syt1 and Ca2+-independent, while fast endocytosis might be regulated by these factors, supporting the notion that different molecular pathways govern the two processes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the differential effects of syt1 KD and Ca2+ on ultrafast versus fast endocytosis.

claim: Ultrafast endocytosis does not involve a clathrin-mediated pathway.
source: Previous reports of ultrafast endocytosis showed that it does not involve a clathrin-mediated pathway (Delvendahl et al., 2016; Watanabe et al., 2013), but it is dependent on actin.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior reports on the molecular mechanisms of ultrafast endocytosis.

claim: Ultrafast endocytosis is dependent on actin.
source: Previous reports of ultrafast endocytosis showed that it does not involve a clathrin-mediated pathway (Delvendahl et al., 2016; Watanabe et al., 2013), but it is dependent on actin.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior reports on the molecular mechanisms of ultrafast endocytosis.

claim: A recent study implicated formins — actin remodeling proteins that serve several cell biological functions — in synaptic vesicle endocytosis in hippocampal synapses as well as at the calyx of Held terminals.
source: In this regard, a recent study implicated formins — actin remodeling proteins that serve several cell biological functions — in synaptic vesicle endocytosis in hippocampal synapses as well as at the calyx of Held terminals (Soykan et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a recent study on formins in endocytosis.

claim: GTP and dynamin independent endocytosis have been proposed to coexist in neurons with dynamin-dependent pathways.
source: Moreover, GTP and dynamin independent endocytosis have been proposed to coexist in neurons with dynamin-dependent pathways (Van Hook and Thoreson, 2012; Xu et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work on dynamin-independent endocytosis.

claim: A novel, still molecularly uncharacterized mechanism may operate independently of the classical endocytic machinery and synchronize synaptic vesicle retrieval with fusion in the timescale of milliseconds.
source: Taken together with our results, this indicates that a novel, still molecularly uncharacterized mechanism may operate independently of the classical endocytic machinery and synchronize synaptic vesicle retrieval with fusion in the timescale of milliseconds.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results and prior literature on endocytic mechanisms.

claim: Around 40% of the fusion events detected were not endocytosed during the imaging period (20 s), indicating that even for single synaptic vesicle exocytosis slow modes of retrieval contribute to synaptic vesicle recycling.
source: Around 40% of the fusion events detected in our experiments were not endocytosed during the imaging period (20 s), indicating that even for single synaptic vesicle exocytosis slow modes of retrieval contribute to synaptic vesicle recycling.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations of non-retrieved events.

claim: Synaptic vesicle proteins undergo localized diffusion after exocytosis, followed by re-clustering and endocytosis.
source: Elegant studies showed that synaptic vesicle proteins undergo localized diffusion after exocytosis, followed by re-clustering and endocytosis (Gimber et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior studies on protein diffusion and re-clustering.

claim: The re-clustering and re-capturing of synaptic vesicle proteins is an extremely slow process, requiring more than 60 s, and it was mediated by the clathrin adaptors CALM and AP-180.
source: The re-clustering and re-capturing of synaptic vesicle proteins is an extremely slow process, requiring more than 60 s, and it was mediated by the clathrin adaptors CALM and AP-180 (Gimber et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work on slow protein re-clustering.

claim: The ultraslow retrieval presented here could be compatible with the mechanism of re-clustering and re-capturing of synaptic vesicle proteins.
source: The ultraslow retrieval presented here could be compatible with this mechanism.
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation linking the observed ultraslow retrieval to prior work on protein re-clustering.

claim: The speed of endocytosis is a limiting step in the maintenance of synaptic transmission under repetitive stimulation.
source: The speed of endocytosis is a limiting step in the maintenance of synaptic transmission under repetitive stimulation (Kavalali, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work on endocytosis as a limiting factor in synaptic transmission.

claim: Synaptic vesicle endocytosis can rapidly replenish vesicle pools and prevent vesicle depletion, while removing the potential hindrance of subsequent fusion events by previously fused vesicles.
source: Synaptic vesicle endocytosis can rapidly replenish vesicle pools and prevent vesicle depletion, while removing the potential hindrance of subsequent fusion events by previously fused vesicles (Fernández-Alfonso and Ryan, 2004; Hua et al., 2013; Sara et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work on the functional importance of endocytosis.

claim: It is plausible to envision the physiological necessity of an ultrafast endocytic mechanism clearing future sites of fusion in preparation for subsequent rounds of neurotransmitter release.
source: Accordingly, it is plausible to envision the physiological necessity of an ultrafast endocytic mechanism clearing future sites of fusion in preparation for subsequent rounds of neurotransmitter release.
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation of the physiological role of ultrafast endocytosis.
